transcript:
Header: Date: 2026-02-18, Start: 3:00 PM PT, Duration: 45 min
Attendees: Elena Park (Redwood AE); Samir Shah (Redwood SE); Maya Lopez (Redwood CSM); Priya Nair (BrightRoute PM); Carlos Mendez (BrightRoute ML Eng); Liam O'Connor (BrightRoute Backend)

Summary: quick review of this week's integration progress, demo of streaming function-calls with structured output, triage of a couple of failing cases, agree on test artifacts to share.

[00:00] Elena: hey everyone, thanks for making time, quick check in before we jump into demos. how's the week at BrightRoute?
[00:18] Priya: pretty busy, thanks. we did a few more integration runs with the SDK, saw better throughput but hit a couple parse errors when using the streaming responses with function calls.
[00:30] Samir: ok that's useful, can you describe the parse errors? is it truncated JSON or unexpected tokens?
[00:39] Carlos: mostly truncated JSON when the stream cuts off mid-object, and sometimes we see an extra comma or small tokenization artifacts, probably a transcription-ish issue but in our app it fails to deserialize.
[00:52] Liam: we also noticed weird ordering when multiple function calls happen in a single session, the client SDK sometimes emits function A then B but our router expects deterministic order.
[01:08] Samir: got it. a couple of notes: streaming can emit partial fragments; recommended pattern is incremental parsing with a final validation pass. we shipped a small helper in the SDK for that — did you use the latest 0.13.2?
[01:25] Priya: we were on 0.12.x, so not the latest.
[01:30] Samir: ok that explains a lot. 0.13.x added buffering and an example for function-call boundaries. i'll email the snippet after this call.
[01:40] Elena: can we demo a quick function-call stream so everyone sees the sequence?
[01:46] Samir: sure, i'll share my screen. single-turn example: user asks to "extract route summary and call external ETA tool" — runtime emits a structured JSON object and a tool_call event.
[02:05] Samir (screen): [demo noisy] streaming chunk 1: "{\"routeSummary\": \"Main St - 12 stops\", \"predictedTime\": \"...\"}"
 then tool_call: {name: "eta_service", args: {lat:..., lon:...}}
[02:30] Priya: that matches what we expected, but in our streams the closing brace was missing for the JSON.
[02:38] Samir: hmm likely your client side parser was fed each newline rather than token-aware; our helper accumulates until a top-level object closes.
[02:50] Liam: also curious about retries: if a tool call fails, what's Redwood's retry behavior?
[02:56] Samir: by default no automatic retries at the platform layer for tool calls — we surface the call failure to the SDK so the app can decide. we can enable simple retry strategies but we generally recommend idempotent design for tools.
[03:12] Carlos: ok we'll implement idempotency and have a retry wrapper on our side.
[03:18] Priya: another thing — structured output schema. we need guaranteed fields: routeId, routeSummary, predictedTimeSecs, confidence. how strict is Redwood about enforcing schema?
[03:30] Samir: the model itself can be prompted to emit strict JSON and we have structured-output utilities in the SDK to validate and coerce types. but it's probabilistic; for strong guarantees we recommend post-validate and fallback generation or using function-calls that return typed args.
[03:46] Priya: function-calls would be better for typed outputs. does that change latency?
[03:52] Samir: minimal overhead, a tiny extra hop if you call an external tool. if you keep logic on the same host (eg local microservice), it's negligible.
[04:05] Elena: let's go over the failing testcases Carlos mentioned — can you share an example request/response?
[04:12] Carlos: yes i'll paste one in the chat, but quickly: request payload ~4k tokens, streaming enabled, model redwood/gpt-3o-quant (example), we got partial JSON at 1:12 into stream, then socket closed.
[04:28] Samir: large payloads + streaming can hit idle timeouts on some client libs; do you use long-poll websockets or SSE?
[04:37] Liam: SSE via the Node SDK.
[04:40] Samir: ok SSE tends to be fine but some proxies close early. we should check proxy timeouts and also ensure the SDK heartbeat is enabled (0.13.x has keepalive).
[04:52] Maya: i'll add a note to troubleshooting doc about keepalive settings.
[05:00] Priya: about model selection: currently using redwood/gpt-3o-quant which is cost-efficient. if we need deterministic structured output should we pick non-quantized or a different variant?
[05:12] Samir: quantization can slightly affect tokenization and rare token distributions; for high fidelity structured output we suggest trying the 'protected' variant or a float16 model for the pilot runs. that will increase cost but improve stability.
[05:28] Carlos: ok we can test float16 for a subset of requests.
[05:33] Priya: any config flags for function-call prioritization? we saw cases where free-text completions were chosen instead of function calls when both were plausible.
[05:44] Samir: yes there's routing hints and function call temperature/sampling knobs in the SDK prompt template; you can bias towards explicit function calls by lowering temperature and adding a pre-prompt that enumerates functions. also we have an explicit 'force_function_call' flag for deterministic behavior.
[06:02] Liam: perfect, we missed that flag.
[06:07] [06:30] Elena: i want to touch on observability — what are you capturing in your logs so Redwood can help debug?
[06:15] Carlos: right now request/response payloads are redacted but we have timestamps, request id, sdk version. we can enable debug logging for a short window.
[06:25] Samir: request IDs are key — please share sample request ids for failing runs. we'll correlate with our backend logs. also, if you can enable full streaming capture (redact PII), that helps us reproduce.
[06:38] Priya: will do. we'll collect three representative failure ids.
[06:44] Samir: another tip: when using function calls + streaming, include function schema in the initial call so the runtime can plan tool invocation earlier.
[06:52] Priya: good call.
[07:00] Carlos: quick question on batching: we thought batching could reduce cost but increases latency. for our route API we need sub-300ms tail latency for interactive users. is batching feasible?
[07:14] Samir: batching helps throughput for many parallel requests but hurts single-request tail latency. for sub-300ms interactive you likely want dedicated capacity and low batch sizes (or no batching), and use the low-latency kernel plan. we can recommend autoscale config.
[07:30] Elena: i can share a config template for dedicated pools targeting 200ms p95.
[07:36] Priya: that would be helpful.
[07:42] [08:00] Samir: demo of SDK snippet for robust parsing (reads code) —
const stream = client.responses.stream({ model: 'redwood/gpt-3o-quant', input, functions: [eta_service_schema], streaming: true });
let buffer = '';
for await (const chunk of stream) {
  buffer += chunk.text;
  try {
    const doc = JSON.parse(buffer);
    handle(doc);
    buffer = '';
  } catch (e) {
    // not a complete JSON yet
  }
}
// final validate with schema

[08:40] Priya: that helps, but we need an example for nested arrays in the schema — will you send a full example?
[08:45] Samir: yes, sending after call.
[08:48] Liam: on the server side we saw ordering issues when multiple function calls invoked the same tool concurrently, we ended up with race conditions updating the cache. any recommendations?
[09:00] Samir: make your tool stateless or add request-scoped ids and optimistic locking. we also support routing tool calls to specific instances if you deploy as a private function in your VPC.
[09:12] Carlos: good note, we'll add request-scoped ids.
[09:18] Priya: security question — for private deployments if we run Redwood Private, how do function calls differ in network topology?
[09:26] Samir: in Redwood Private, function calls can be proxied internally; tool invocations never leave your VPC by default. we can enable service mesh integrations or direct private endpoints.
[09:38] Priya: great. we'll consider that for sensitive data.
[09:43] Elena: back to next steps, we want to schedule a latency benchmark. what inputs do you need?
[09:49] Samir: sample payloads (the 95th percentile size), concurrency targets, and whether you want streaming enabled. also desired p95 SLA.
[09:58] Priya: we'll share sample payloads and target p95=300ms by end of week.
[10:04] Maya: i'll coordinate scheduling and get a shared spreadsheet for the benchmark runs.
[10:12] Carlos: also will share the three failure request ids and a few sample request/response captures.
[10:18] Samir: perfect. i'll prepare a checklist: update to SDK 0.13.x, enable keepalive, try float16 model for structured-critical flows, use force_function_call where determinism needed, and run smoke tests.
[10:33] Elena: i'll also include pricing guidance in the follow-up email for dedicated capacity options given their latency needs.
[10:40] Priya: thanks, that helps frame decisions.
[10:46] Elena: any other blockers?
[10:50] Liam: nothing blocking, just need those snippets and the structured schema examples.
[10:55] Priya: we should aim for the next sync same time next week — ok?
[10:59] Elena: yes will send calendar.
[11:05] Close: thanks everyone.

Notes: occasional transcription artifacts in chunk text and function names (e.g., "etna_service" vs "eta_service"). shared artifacts: SDK snippet (link posted in chat), benchmark spreadsheet (link to drive), structured-output schema examples (attached).
